correctness.rationale: There are exactly 20 possible edges on six vertices. All five-vertex injections of F5 produce precisely 180 distinct forbidden 3-edge masks. An independently written complete traversal of all 2^20=1,048,576 labeled hypergraphs tested each candidate for containing a forbidden mask and found maximum 10 and precisely six labeled maximizers; all six are stars centered at each vertex. The explicit star is F5-free because a star center would have to be in the shared pair of the first two F5 edges, but the third edge excludes that pair. The finite check covers the *entire* domain n=6; no random sampling, timeout inference or asymptotic extrapolation is used.

evidence: Liu, On a hypergraph Mantel theorem, concerns the eventual n-dependent F5 extremum.
The 2026 blow-up study records a previously known large-order F5 threshold n>=33, while the Andrasfai–Erdos–Sos-type work assumes minimum-degree hypotheses.
broader_coverage.reasoning: For n=6 the claimed star has 10 triples, whereas the balanced complete tripartite 3-graph on six vertices has 8. Therefore a large-n tripartite extremal theorem cannot imply the small-order star formula. Minimum-degree and cancellative-subclass statements also do not directly classify every F5-free six-vertex hypergraph.

evidence: Eventually the F5 extremum is balanced tripartite, giving 8 edges at six vertices if one naively specializes—strictly below the exhibited 10-edge star.
Independent full 2^20 enumeration establishes upper-bound and uniqueness not supplied by large-order hypotheses.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Specializing an eventual theorem to n=6 is invalid because n is outside its valid range. The exact six-vertex bound is not a routine numerical evaluation of a known all-n formula in inspected sources; a genuinely all-n stronger theorem would cover it, but none was identified.

evidence: F5 is the generalized 3-uniform triangle with edges {abc,abd,cde}, not the tight cycle C5^(3) (also five vertices but five edges).
Resultary returned a C5^(3)-free six-vertex census with different forbidden configuration and extremum; it cannot imply this F5 result.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Generalized-triangle / cancellative hypergraph terminology must be distinguished from tight-five-cycle and induced-subgraph avoidance. The claimed ex3(6,F5)=10 is a non-induced forbidden-configuration statement.

originality.rationale: The classical eventual Turán theorem gives a balanced complete tripartite extremum only for sufficiently large n; the available modern sources explicitly discuss eventual n thresholds, not the six-vertex star exception and unique extremizers. Search did not locate a precise earlier n=6 table. This qualified novelty is limited by uninspected older Frankl–Füredi full text or possible small-hypergraph catalogs.
residual_risks: A prior computational small-hypergraph table or the uninspected 1983 source could already include the six-vertex exact maximum.
As a narrow n=6 classification its impact is limited; no general upper bound or uniqueness for n>=7 follows.

value.rationale: This is the first small-order regime immediately beyond the five-vertex F5 pattern where the extremal family is a genuine star, unlike the balanced tripartite 6-vertex construction with only eight triples. The exact smallest nontrivial endpoint and uniqueness classification are natural base-case extremal hypergraph invariants that a later small-order classification or stability argument can cite. The small size and lack of a general n-theorem limit significance, but do not make this unknown exact natural finite case mathematically arbitrary.

limitations: Non-induced F5-free triple systems only, exactly six vertices.
No extrapolation to general Turán numbers, balanced tripartite extremality or other forbidden 5-vertex patterns.
